what: The sections of this article, each with a line and a paragraph, for showing what the reader has already read. Built by admin/build/summaries.py from admin/content/articles/summaries/.

sections.label: The opening
sections.line: AI lets domain experts build their own startups
sections.para: For twenty years outsiders with capital built winning startups, then became the incumbents. Agents now let people who know the problem build it themselves; the fastest-growing US startups are founded at a mean age of 45. This favours Europe's see-it-working investors, shown through three founders in security, knee health and legal transcription.

sections.label: In short
sections.line: Execution got cheap, so experts can now start
sections.para: Outsiders with capital displaced incumbents, then became them. Agents now do most of the building, a third of new US startups have a single founder, and experts were always the better bet: mean founding age 45, with industry experience doubling the odds. Later, sceptical European money suits founders who can build first.

sections.label: The playbook that worked
sections.line: Outsiders with capital displaced better-placed incumbents
sections.para: Clever, ambitious outsiders found a gap, did the hundred calls, raised money and hired the experts, displacing incumbents who had customers and knowledge but lacked structure and technology culture. Venture is a portfolio: in Horsley Bridge's data on about 7,000 deals, 6% produced at least 10x and made up 60% of returns.

sections.label: This is not a criticism
sections.line: Outsiders changed industries, though the theory is imperfect
sections.para: These companies changed industries, and Christensen found disk-drive disruptors were always entrants. The evidence is untidy: of 77 cases reviewed, only 7 fitted the theory fully. Talent was often inside incumbents already, as Adrian Cockcroft told a Fortune 100 CTO: Netflix hired them from you, and got out of their way.

sections.label: Then they became the incumbents
sections.line: Disruptors fade into the incumbents they once displaced
sections.para: Agility fades until disruptors resemble what they replaced, as Simon Wardley described. Older firms produce lower-quality technology, merger novelty falls about 60%, and 5.3% to 7.4% of drug acquisitions were killer acquisitions. Workers toggle apps about 1,200 times a day, and organisations juggle 83 security tools from 29 vendors.

sections.label: Execution just got cheap
sections.line: Agents removed the millions once needed to start
sections.para: With agents, one person who knows what to build can do what needed a funded team. Solo-founder startups rose from 23.7% in 2019 to 36.3% in early 2025; top AI companies on Stripe hit $1 million in a median 11.5 months. These are the fastest, not average, but the direction is clear.

sections.label: The experts were always the better bet
sections.line: Successful founders are middle-aged industry experts, not outsiders
sections.para: A study of 2.7 million US founders found the fastest-growing 1 in 1,000 ventures had a mean founding age of 45.0. Three or more years in the same industry doubled the rate of top-tier growth. Experts lacked access to capital and engineers, not knowledge, and that part got cheap.

sections.label: Three expert founders
sections.line: Three founders build from deep knowledge of their field
sections.para: I build sgit.ai and RiskMandate from security and CISO experience, after The Cyber Boardroom paused; agents wrote most of SG/Send's 4,476 commits. Knee surgeon Chinmay Gupte builds OmKneeHealth and My Knee Score, and Kate Curtis-Evans builds Audio Genius for legal transcription. Their narrow focus is now an advantage.

sections.label: Why this favours Europe
sections.line: Europe's cautious money suits founders who build first
sections.para: European companies raise at higher revenue and lower valuations, per Equidam. Since 74% of high-growth startups fail from premature scaling, sceptical money suits experts who build first, and Atomico finds Europe equally capital efficient. Open source policy and impact funding fit, but Europe raises just 5% of global VC and scales poorly.

sections.label: What this does not claim
sections.line: Outsiders still matter; the Europe evidence is weak
sections.para: Outsiders are not finished; experts can now start too. AI growth figures are the fastest, not typical, and the Europe comparison rests on one vendor's data, with no software satisfaction survey found. I help two of the founders, Kate's details were added on 15 October, and I have a stake.

sections.label: Where this comes from
sections.line: Sources: founder studies, VC reports and research papers
sections.para: Based on my memo of 15 October 2026, checked by three research agents. Sources include Azoulay and colleagues on founder age, Carta, Stripe, Bessemer, Startup Genome, CB Insights, Equidam, Atomico, the Draghi report, Dealroom, Benedict Evans, Christensen, Wardley, killer acquisitions research, Panaseer, and the founders' public pages.
